screens.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation and Deallocation
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how to request and release heap memory in C++ using the new and delete operators, and their array counterparts new[] and delete[]. This matters a lot in game development because object counts and lifetimes change at runtime — enemies spawn, levels load, particle systems expand — and the heap lets you create and destroy objects on demand. I'll show you the precise rule you must never forget: match single-object allocation with delete, and array allocation with delete[]; failing to match them leads to undefined behavior, resource leaks, or crashes. We'll walk through practical examples: allocating a single Enemy, allocating an array of Enemy objects, a simple GameObject manager that deletes its contents at level end, and two common runtime errors — memory leaks and double deletion — with concrete code snippets you can run and inspect. You'll also see defensive patterns like setting pointers to nullptr after deletion and iterating containers of raw pointers safely. By the end you'll understand not only how these operators work, but why the rules exist and how to spot the bugs they cause.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to allocate and deallocate heap memory safely, work with both single objects and arrays, and recognize the common errors that plague manual memory management. First, you will learn the mechanics of the new operator — how it requests memory, constructs an object, and returns a pointer — and why delete must be called to invoke the destructor and free that memory. Second, you'll practice new[] and delete[] for arrays, understanding that constructors and destructors are invoked for each element. Third, you'll learn defensive practices such as setting pointers to nullptr after deletion and checking for nullptr before dereferencing to avoid dangling pointers. Fourth, you'll be able to identify memory leaks and double deletions in simple game code and apply correct fixes. These skills matter in games because improper heap management leads to steadily growing memory use, crashes, or corrupted game state, and you will practice examples that mirror real game systems like spawn managers and level teardown.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Diagnostics
screens.narratorSegment: In addition to writing correct allocation code, you will practice patterns that appear frequently in games: managers that own dynamic objects, loops that allocate multiple entities, and teardown functions that must free every pointer. You'll also learn simple diagnostics: printing messages in constructors and destructors to verify creation and destruction, running short leak demos where a temporary object is never deleted, and a controlled double deletion test to observe undefined behavior hazards. These exercises are deliberately small so you can see the lifecycle of objects in the console: creation messages when new runs, destructor messages when delete runs, and missing destructor calls when memory is leaked. We'll also add defensive checks like if (ptr) before dereferencing and immediate ptr = nullptr after delete to eliminate dangling references. Practicing these diagnostics helps you catch leaks and mismatches early, and prepares you for the next chapter where smart pointers automate many of these responsibilities.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Practice & Diagnostics
Diagnostic patterns
  • Log creation/destruction messages in constructors and destructors to observe lifecycle.
  • Create small functions that intentionally leak so you can see memory growth locally.
  • Simulate double deletion in a controlled way and then restore ptr = nullptr after delete.
Example console output
Enemy Goblin created on heap.
Enemy Goblin attacks!
Enemy Goblin destroyed from heap.
Quick checklist
• Every new must have a paired delete or delete[]
• After delete set pointer to nullptr
• Check for nullptr before dereference
Verified practice

screens.title: Allocating a Single Object with new
screens.narratorSegment: Let's examine what happens when you allocate a single object with new. The operator requests a block of memory large enough for the requested type, constructs that object in place by calling its constructor, and returns a pointer to the newly created object. In game code this is how you spawn a single enemy or a player when the size is known at runtime. For example, when you write new Enemy("Goblin", 50) the Enemy constructor runs and you can immediately call methods through the returned pointer. Importantly, the memory stays allocated until you call delete on that pointer, which calls the destructor and frees the memory. A common misconception is thinking new only reserves raw bytes; in C++ it also runs constructors. Another misunderstanding is assuming automatic cleanup; unlike local stack objects, heap objects persist beyond scope and must be deleted by the owner. A practical tip is that the allocating code should own deletion responsibility or transfer ownership explicitly. In the code panel you'll see a concise example: allocate, use, then delete and set the pointer to nullptr to avoid dangling references. After you delete, any further use is undefined behavior, so always guard and nullify. Do you have a clear owner for every heap allocation in your game systems?

keyIdea.title: Single-object allocation
keyIdea.text: new constructs and returns a pointer; delete must be called by the owning code to run the destructor and free memory.

content.html:
Core Concept
Allocate a single object
new allocates memory, calls the constructor, and returns a pointer you use until you delete it.
class Enemy {
public:
  std::string type;
  int health;
  Enemy(std::string t, int h) : type(t), health(h) {
    std::cout << "Enemy " << type << " created on heap.
";
  }
  ~Enemy() { std::cout << "Enemy " << type << " destroyed from heap.
"; }
  void attack() { std::cout << type << " attacks!
"; }
};

// Allocate a single Enemy object on the heap
Enemy* goblin = new Enemy("Goblin", 50);
goblin->attack();

// ... use goblin ...

delete goblin;          // Deallocate
goblin = nullptr;      // Avoid dangling pointer
Explanation
  • new allocates heap memory and calls the constructor in the allocated space.
  • delete calls the destructor and then frees the memory back to the heap.
  • After delete the pointer becomes invalid; set it to nullptr to avoid accidental use.
Example scenario
Spawn a single boss when the player reaches a landmark. Allocate on spawn and delete when the boss dies or the level unloads.
Key Takeaway

Owning code must pair every new with a delete and clearly own the object's lifecycle.

screens.title: Deallocation with delete and destructors
screens.narratorSegment: Delete does two things in C++: it invokes the object's destructor so the object can release its owned resources, and it returns the memory block to the heap allocator. That destructor call is essential when an object manages other resources — open files, allocated buffers, or game assets — because only the destructor knows how to clean them up. A subtle misconception is that delete only frees bytes; in reality destructors run first and must be matched to the constructor's work. If you call delete on a pointer to a polymorphic type, ensure the destructor is virtual in the base class so the correct derived destructor runs. Another mistake is deleting memory that wasn't allocated with new; that is undefined behavior. In this example code we explicitly delete the goblin pointer and then set it to nullptr to prevent later accidental dereference. For managers that hold many pointers, the destructor often iterates through a container and deletes each element. That pattern centralizes cleanup at level end and ensures destructors execute for each object. Finally, after delete you must not access the object; doing so is undefined and often leads to crashes. Consider question: who owns deletion in your systems?

keyIdea.title: Delete runs destructors
keyIdea.text: delete first runs the destructor to release resources, then frees memory. Always ensure ownership and virtual destructors for polymorphic types.

content.html:
Definition
delete calls destructors and frees memory
Destructors undo what the constructor did: release asset handles, free owned memory, and perform tidy-up logic.
// Deallocate the goblin
delete goblin;        // Calls ~Enemy(), then frees memory
goblin = nullptr;    // Avoid dangling pointer

// Example manager cleanup (see later lessons):
for (Enemy* e : activeEnemies) {
  delete e; // ensure each enemy's destructor runs
}
activeEnemies.clear();
When destructor is critical
  • Objects that own dynamic buffers, file handles, or GPU resources must free them in the destructor.
  • If base class destructors are not virtual, derived destructors may not run on delete via base pointer.
Common mistake
Deleting memory twice or deleting memory not allocated with new causes undefined behavior and possible crashes.
Key Takeaway

Make destructors do cleanup and ensure the correct destructor runs by using virtual destructors for polymorphic bases.

screens.title: Arrays on the Heap: new[] and delete[]
screens.narratorSegment: When you need multiple objects whose count is known only at runtime, use new[] to allocate an array of objects on the heap. new[] allocates a contiguous block large enough for N objects and calls each default constructor, so every element is a fully constructed object you can use with array syntax like enemies[i]. Because each element's destructor must run when the array is released, you must call delete[] to deallocate memory. Using plain delete on an array is a common and dangerous mistake: it can call only the first destructor and then free the memory incorrectly, producing undefined behavior, leaks, or later memory corruption. A typical game use is spawning a particle buffer or an initial pool of enemies. In practice, prefer container classes or smart pointers, but understanding new[] and delete[] is essential. The example demonstrates allocating an array, setting some fields, iterating to use objects, and then delete[] with a nullptr assignment. A common misconception is that arrays of objects behave like primitive arrays; remember constructors and destructors run per element. Always match new[] with delete[] to ensure correct destruction for every element.

keyIdea.title: Array allocation rule
keyIdea.text: Use new[] to allocate arrays and delete[] to deallocate; mismatching leads to undefined behavior because destructors may not run for every element.

content.html:
Process Flow
Allocate and deallocate arrays
new[] constructs each element; delete[] calls the destructor for every element before freeing memory.
// Allocate an array of 5 Enemy objects on the heap
Enemy* enemies = new Enemy[5]; // default constructors called for each element

// Use array-like syntax
enemies[0].type = "Orc";
enemies[0].health = 100;
enemies[1].type = "Skeleton";
enemies[1].health = 30;

// ... use enemies ...

// Correct deallocation:
delete[] enemies; // Calls destructor for each element
enemies = nullptr;
Explanation
new[] reserves a contiguous block and runs constructors. delete[] ensures every destructor runs. Mismatches are undefined behavior.
Analogy
Think of new[] as booking seats in a row and assigning each passenger a seat; delete[] must let every passenger off in order.
Key Takeaway

Always match new[] with delete[] so every element's destructor runs and resources are cleaned up.

screens.title: Matching Pairs: new/delete vs new[]/delete[]
screens.narratorSegment: The central rule of manual heap management in C++ is simple to state but easy to violate: match new with delete, and new[] with delete[]. This exists because single-object new and array new[] may store different bookkeeping information, and because destructors must run for each constructed element in an array. If you mix them up, you enter undefined behavior territory. In practice, that can mean only the first object's destructor runs or memory is freed incorrectly, causing leaks or heap corruption. To apply the rule correctly in your codebase, give ownership to a single responsible component — often a manager or container — and make that component perform the matching deallocation. For example, if a spawn function uses new[] to create many objects, its corresponding teardown must call delete[]. Contrast this with allocating a single object for a unique boss — use new and delete. When traversing a vector of raw pointers, call delete on each pointer individually if each pointer was allocated with new. A common debugging trick is to instrument constructors and destructors with logs to confirm correct pairing at runtime. The takeaway: clear ownership and strict pairing prevent severe runtime bugs.

keyIdea.title: Pairing rule
keyIdea.text: The memory and destructor behavior differ for single and array allocations; matching them prevents undefined behavior and resource corruption.

content.html:
Comparison
new / delete
Used for single objects. Calls constructor on allocation and destructor on delete.
Example
Enemy* e = new Enemy("Orc",80); // ... delete e;
Comparison
new[] / delete[]
Used for arrays of objects. Each element's constructor and destructor run.
Example
Enemy* arr = new Enemy[3]; // ... delete[] arr;
Debugging tip
Instrument constructors and destructors with logs. If destructors are missing for some elements, re-check your pairing and ownership.

screens.title: Manager Pattern: Owning and Cleaning Up Dynamic Objects
screens.narratorSegment: In game code it's common for a manager to own dynamic objects and take responsibility for their deallocation when a level ends. The manager pattern centralizes memory ownership and prevents scattered delete calls across the codebase. In the provided example, GameObjectManager holds a std::vector of Enemy* pointers. spawnEnemy calls new to create enemies and pushes the pointer into the vector. The manager's destructor iterates over the vector, calls delete on each pointer, and clears the vector. This guarantees destructors run for every object and avoids leaks when the manager goes out of scope. A key practice is to check pointers for nullptr before dereferencing inside update loops. Note one subtlety: if a manager is destroyed during shutdown it must still perform cleanup — relying on automatic program termination is not robust. Also avoid double deletion by setting each element to nullptr after deletion or clearing the vector fully. Eventually you'll replace raw pointers with smart pointers for safer ownership, but knowing how managers work clarifies why smart pointers are designed the way they are. Manager Pattern: Owning and Cleaning Up Dynamic Objects means managers should own allocations and ensure all owned pointers are deleted at teardown to prevent leaks and enforce correct destructor calls.. In practical terms, a gameobjectmanager responsible for allocating and deleting objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Centralized ownership
keyIdea.text: Managers should own allocations and ensure all owned pointers are deleted at teardown to prevent leaks and enforce correct destructor calls.

content.html:
Process Flow
GameObjectManager example
class GameObjectManager {
public:
  std::vector<Enemy*> activeEnemies;

  void spawnEnemy(std::string type, int health) {
    Enemy* newEnemy = new Enemy(type, health);
    activeEnemies.push_back(newEnemy);
  }

  ~GameObjectManager() {
    for (Enemy* enemy : activeEnemies) {
      delete enemy;
    }
    activeEnemies.clear();
  }
};
Why managers help
  • Centralize allocation and deallocation so ownership is clear.
  • Make it easy to perform batch cleanup when levels end or a scene unloads.
  • Reduce accidental double deletions by clearing the container after deletion.
Practical note
When possible, prefer smart pointers inside containers to express ownership and avoid manual delete calls.
Key Takeaway

A manager that owns allocations makes teardown predictable — delete each owned object in one place.

screens.title: Memory Leak: What it is and how to spot it
screens.narratorSegment: A memory leak happens when allocated memory is never released back to the system because delete or delete[] was not called. In a long-running game this means R A M usage climbs over time, which can slow down the game or eventually cause an out-of-memory crash. You might see a leak when a temporary helper function uses new without a matching delete, or when a manager forgot to delete objects during a level transition. Spotting leaks starts with small experiments: instrument constructors and destructors with log messages and run the code path that should free memory; if destructor messages don't appear, you likely have a leak. The chapter includes a demonstration function that intentionally creates a temporary character with new and never deletes it; this produces a visible footprint in the task-manager-style visualization described in the live coding brief. To prevent leaks, adopt a clear ownership model: whoever allocates should document or transfer ownership, and managers should clean up in their destructor. Later, smart pointers will automate this pattern, but first practice noticing leaks by watching for missing destructor messages or steadily increasing memory usage during repeated level loads.

keyIdea.title: Memory Leak
keyIdea.text: A leak occurs when allocated memory is not deallocated; detect by missing destructor calls or rising memory use, and fix by ensuring ownership and cleanup.

content.html:
Definition
Memory Leak
Memory allocated on the heap that is never freed. Over time this consumes program memory.
Intentional leak example
void createTemporaryCharacterLeak() { Character* tempCharacter = new Character("Ghost", 10); std::cout << "Created temporary character (will leak). "; // forgot to delete tempCharacter here — this leaks memory }
Symptoms
Growing memory usage over repeated actions, missing destructor logs, or crashes after long play sessions.
How to fix
  • Identify the owner and ensure it calls delete or delete[].
  • Use instrumentation and repeat the scenario to confirm destructors run.
  • Prefer RAII and smart pointers in future code to avoid manual leaks.
Key Takeaway

Leaked memory is avoidable with clear ownership and explicit cleanup; instrument destructors to verify correct behavior.

screens.title: Double Deletion and Dangling Pointers
screens.narratorSegment: Double deletion occurs when you call delete or delete[] on a pointer whose memory has already been freed. After the first delete the pointer becomes a dangling pointer — it still holds the old address but the memory there is no longer valid. A second delete tries to free memory that has already been returned to the heap, which is undefined behavior and often leads to immediate crashes or later corruption. A common defensive step is to set the pointer to nullptr immediately after deletion; deleting nullptr is safe and has no effect. When working with containers of pointers, be careful to avoid patterns that can cause double deletion: do not delete an object in two separate managers, and when transferring ownership make that transfer explicit so only the new owner deletes. Another helpful approach is to clear pointer containers after deletion so no stale pointers remain. In debugging, run a small double-delete experiment in a controlled environment to see how it behaves, but remove or guard the code in production. The long-term solution is to adopt smart pointers which enforce single ownership or reference counting.

content.html:
Comparison
Double Deletion & Dangling Pointers
After delete the pointer might still hold an address; using it or deleting again is unsafe.
Character* testChar = new Character("Test", 10); delete testChar; // testChar still points at freed memory // delete testChar; // Double delete — DANGER! testChar = nullptr; // Safe defensive step
Common causes
Two owners both calling delete, forgetting to nullify after deletion, or deleting after moving ownership without updating references.
Defensive steps
  • Set pointers to nullptr immediately after delete.
  • Clear containers after deleting their elements.
  • Document and enforce single ownership; use smart pointers where appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Never assume deletion is harmless twice; nullify pointers and adopt clear ownership to avoid undefined behavior.

screens.title: Safe Deallocation Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Use a short checklist each time you perform manual deallocation to prevent leaks and double deletes. Start by identifying the owner — determine which object or system is responsible for deletion. If the pointer may be null, check it before dereferencing or deleting. After calling delete or delete[] always set the pointer to nullptr and, if the pointer is in a container, remove or clear that container entry. If you're deleting many objects in a loop, ensure you use the correct operator: delete for single allocations and delete[] for arrays. Instrument the constructor and destructor to emit logs during development so you can validate that destructors run at teardown. When transferring ownership, document the transfer explicitly and avoid implicit shared ownership of raw pointers. Finally, plan for exceptions: if a function that allocates can throw, use RAII or smart pointers to guarantee cleanup in error paths. Practicing this checklist on small examples until it becomes second nature will greatly reduce runtime memory issues in your game systems. screens.title: Assessment: Allocating and Deallocating Tiles

content.html:
Assessment
Allocate and deallocate 100 Tiles
void manageTiles() {
  std::vector<Tile*> levelTiles;
  const int numTiles = 100;

  // Allocation
  for (int i = 0; i < numTiles; ++i) {
    levelTiles.push_back(new Tile(i));
  }

  // Deallocation
  for (Tile* tilePtr : levelTiles) {
    delete tilePtr;
  }
  levelTiles.clear();
}
Common mistakes
  • Using delete[] on the vector or forgetting to delete each Tile*.
  • Deleting elements but not clearing the vector, leaving dangling pointers.
Why this matters
Tile allocation is a microcosm of larger object management problems: correct bulk cleanup scales to many systems in a game.
Key Takeaway

Always delete what you new, and clear containers to avoid dangling pointers and leaks.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the most important technical points from this chapter. First, the new operator allocates heap memory and runs the object's constructor; delete runs the destructor and frees memory. Second, arrays allocated with new[] construct each element and require delete[] when freeing; mixing delete and delete[] causes undefined behavior. Third, memory leaks occur when allocated memory is never freed and can be detected by missing destructor logs or rising memory use; fix leaks by ensuring the owner calls delete. These concise concepts form the foundation of safe manual memory management. As you progress, you'll replace many manual patterns with smart pointers, but these rules and diagnostic techniques are essential to understand what smart pointers automate and why they prevent classes of bugs. Keep these core ideas in mind as you write and review game systems that allocate and free objects at runtime.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to request and release heap memory in C++ using the new and delete operators, and their array counterparts new[] and delete[]. This matters a lot in game development because object counts and lifetimes change at runtime — enemies spawn, levels load, particle systems expand — and the heap lets you create and destroy objects on demand. I'll show you the precise rule you must never forget: match single-object allocation with delete, and array allocation with delete[]; failing to match them leads to undefined behavior, resource leaks, or crashes. We'll walk through practical examples: allocating a single Enemy, allocating an array of Enemy objects, a simple GameObject manager that deletes its contents at level end, and two common runtime errors — memory leaks and double deletion — with concrete code snippets you can run and inspect. You'll also see defensive patterns like setting pointers to nullptr after deletion and iterating containers of raw pointers safely. By the end you'll understand not only how these operators work, but why the rules exist and how to spot the bugs they cause.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to allocate and deallocate heap memory safely, work with both single objects and arrays, and recognize the common errors that plague manual memory management. First, you will learn the mechanics of the new operator — how it requests memory, constructs an object, and returns a pointer — and why delete must be called to invoke the destructor and free that memory. Second, you'll practice new[] and delete[] for arrays, understanding that constructors and destructors are invoked for each element. Third, you'll learn defensive practices such as setting pointers to nullptr after deletion and checking for nullptr before dereferencing to avoid dangling pointers. Fourth, you'll be able to identify memory leaks and double deletions in simple game code and apply correct fixes. These skills matter in games because improper heap management leads to steadily growing memory use, crashes, or corrupted game state, and you will practice examples that mirror real game systems like spawn managers and level teardown.

In addition to writing correct allocation code, you will practice patterns that appear frequently in games: managers that own dynamic objects, loops that allocate multiple entities, and teardown functions that must free every pointer. You'll also learn simple diagnostics: printing messages in constructors and destructors to verify creation and destruction, running short leak demos where a temporary object is never deleted, and a controlled double deletion test to observe undefined behavior hazards. These exercises are deliberately small so you can see the lifecycle of objects in the console: creation messages when new runs, destructor messages when delete runs, and missing destructor calls when memory is leaked. We'll also add defensive checks like if (ptr) before dereferencing and immediate ptr = nullptr after delete to eliminate dangling references. Practicing these diagnostics helps you catch leaks and mismatches early, and prepares you for the next chapter where smart pointers automate many of these responsibilities.

Let's examine what happens when you allocate a single object with new. The operator requests a block of memory large enough for the requested type, constructs that object in place by calling its constructor, and returns a pointer to the newly created object. In game code this is how you spawn a single enemy or a player when the size is known at runtime. For example, when you write new Enemy("Goblin", 50) the Enemy constructor runs and you can immediately call methods through the returned pointer. Importantly, the memory stays allocated until you call delete on that pointer, which calls the destructor and frees the memory. A common misconception is thinking new only reserves raw bytes; in C++ it also runs constructors. Another misunderstanding is assuming automatic cleanup; unlike local stack objects, heap objects persist beyond scope and must be deleted by the owner. A practical tip is that the allocating code should own deletion responsibility or transfer ownership explicitly. In the code panel you'll see a concise example: allocate, use, then delete and set the pointer to nullptr to avoid dangling references. After you delete, any further use is undefined behavior, so always guard and nullify. Do you have a clear owner for every heap allocation in your game systems?

Delete does two things in C++: it invokes the object's destructor so the object can release its owned resources, and it returns the memory block to the heap allocator. That destructor call is essential when an object manages other resources — open files, allocated buffers, or game assets — because only the destructor knows how to clean them up. A subtle misconception is that delete only frees bytes; in reality destructors run first and must be matched to the constructor's work. If you call delete on a pointer to a polymorphic type, ensure the destructor is virtual in the base class so the correct derived destructor runs. Another mistake is deleting memory that wasn't allocated with new; that is undefined behavior. In this example code we explicitly delete the goblin pointer and then set it to nullptr to prevent later accidental dereference. For managers that hold many pointers, the destructor often iterates through a container and deletes each element. That pattern centralizes cleanup at level end and ensures destructors execute for each object. Finally, after delete you must not access the object; doing so is undefined and often leads to crashes. Consider question: who owns deletion in your systems?

When you need multiple objects whose count is known only at runtime, use new[] to allocate an array of objects on the heap. new[] allocates a contiguous block large enough for N objects and calls each default constructor, so every element is a fully constructed object you can use with array syntax like enemies[i]. Because each element's destructor must run when the array is released, you must call delete[] to deallocate memory. Using plain delete on an array is a common and dangerous mistake: it can call only the first destructor and then free the memory incorrectly, producing undefined behavior, leaks, or later memory corruption. A typical game use is spawning a particle buffer or an initial pool of enemies. In practice, prefer container classes or smart pointers, but understanding new[] and delete[] is essential. The example demonstrates allocating an array, setting some fields, iterating to use objects, and then delete[] with a nullptr assignment. A common misconception is that arrays of objects behave like primitive arrays; remember constructors and destructors run per element. Always match new[] with delete[] to ensure correct destruction for every element.

The central rule of manual heap management in C++ is simple to state but easy to violate: match new with delete, and new[] with delete[]. This exists because single-object new and array new[] may store different bookkeeping information, and because destructors must run for each constructed element in an array. If you mix them up, you enter undefined behavior territory. In practice, that can mean only the first object's destructor runs or memory is freed incorrectly, causing leaks or heap corruption. To apply the rule correctly in your codebase, give ownership to a single responsible component — often a manager or container — and make that component perform the matching deallocation. For example, if a spawn function uses new[] to create many objects, its corresponding teardown must call delete[]. Contrast this with allocating a single object for a unique boss — use new and delete. When traversing a vector of raw pointers, call delete on each pointer individually if each pointer was allocated with new. A common debugging trick is to instrument constructors and destructors with logs to confirm correct pairing at runtime. The takeaway: clear ownership and strict pairing prevent severe runtime bugs.

In game code it's common for a manager to own dynamic objects and take responsibility for their deallocation when a level ends. The manager pattern centralizes memory ownership and prevents scattered delete calls across the codebase. In the provided example, GameObjectManager holds a std::vector of Enemy* pointers. spawnEnemy calls new to create enemies and pushes the pointer into the vector. The manager's destructor iterates over the vector, calls delete on each pointer, and clears the vector. This guarantees destructors run for every object and avoids leaks when the manager goes out of scope. A key practice is to check pointers for nullptr before dereferencing inside update loops. Note one subtlety: if a manager is destroyed during shutdown it must still perform cleanup — relying on automatic program termination is not robust. Also avoid double deletion by setting each element to nullptr after deletion or clearing the vector fully. Eventually you'll replace raw pointers with smart pointers for safer ownership, but knowing how managers work clarifies why smart pointers are designed the way they are. Manager Pattern: Owning and Cleaning Up Dynamic Objects means managers should own allocations and ensure all owned pointers are deleted at teardown to prevent leaks and enforce correct destructor calls.. In practical terms, a gameobjectmanager responsible for allocating and deleting objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A memory leak happens when allocated memory is never released back to the system because delete or delete[] was not called. In a long-running game this means R A M usage climbs over time, which can slow down the game or eventually cause an out-of-memory crash. You might see a leak when a temporary helper function uses new without a matching delete, or when a manager forgot to delete objects during a level transition. Spotting leaks starts with small experiments: instrument constructors and destructors with log messages and run the code path that should free memory; if destructor messages don't appear, you likely have a leak. The chapter includes a demonstration function that intentionally creates a temporary character with new and never deletes it; this produces a visible footprint in the task-manager-style visualization described in the live coding brief. To prevent leaks, adopt a clear ownership model: whoever allocates should document or transfer ownership, and managers should clean up in their destructor. Later, smart pointers will automate this pattern, but first practice noticing leaks by watching for missing destructor messages or steadily increasing memory usage during repeated level loads.

Double deletion occurs when you call delete or delete[] on a pointer whose memory has already been freed. After the first delete the pointer becomes a dangling pointer — it still holds the old address but the memory there is no longer valid. A second delete tries to free memory that has already been returned to the heap, which is undefined behavior and often leads to immediate crashes or later corruption. A common defensive step is to set the pointer to nullptr immediately after deletion; deleting nullptr is safe and has no effect. When working with containers of pointers, be careful to avoid patterns that can cause double deletion: do not delete an object in two separate managers, and when transferring ownership make that transfer explicit so only the new owner deletes. Another helpful approach is to clear pointer containers after deletion so no stale pointers remain. In debugging, run a small double-delete experiment in a controlled environment to see how it behaves, but remove or guard the code in production. The long-term solution is to adopt smart pointers which enforce single ownership or reference counting.
